newsitem.title: USA: USDA trade advisor sees subsidy issue lingering.
newsitem.headline: USDA trade advisor sees subsidy issue lingering.

text.p: The recently revived issue between the United States and the European Union of grain export subsidies is not likely to go away soon, said the Agriculture Department's senior trade advisor Paul Drazek.

In an interview with Reuters on Friday, Drazek said that he discussed the use of subsidies at length last week with EU officials in Brussels, and said it is clear that Europe intends to continue subsidizing its grain exports as long as it feels it necessary.
"I received no hint from them (EU officials) that they intended or would have any intentions whatsoever of ending export subsidies," said Drazek.

Drazek said that while officials in Brussels assured him that the EU does not want to undercut the United States, or use the subsidies in a "predatory" way, Washington still disagrees with the EU's premise that the subsidies are necessary and justifiable at this point in time.

"They should adjust their domestic price so that they don't need export subsidies," said Drazek. "In principle we cannot accept any argument that countries have to use subsidies, so the fact that countries are using export subsidies suggests that there is a structural flaw."

Drazek said he told EU officials that Washington disagreed with its use of subsidies, and reiterated that the United States will be closely monitoring EU's activities and will resort to using its own subsidies if U.S. exports are impacted by EU's sales practices.

"If we determine that their use of subsidies is having an adverse effect on our market and on our ability to compete in the world markets, we would certainly have no choice but to respond. That's the message I delivered," said Drazek.
"That implies very very close ongoing scrutiny of European activities, and at some point, it may be our determination that their use of export subsidies has crossed the line," he said.

Drazek also discussed the issue of genetically-altered crops, especially soybeans and corn, with various EU officials, and said he senses a growing acceptance "among people who understand the issue" that gene-altered products should be approved, but said EU's scientific community has to do a better job of informing consumers on the issue.
An EU scientific panel is reviewing a genetically-altered corn developed by Ciba-Geigy Corp, and Drazek said he expects their work to be completed this year, possibly even within the next month.
He is hopeful that approval will be obtained in time to avoid any disruption in the trade of this year's U.S. corn crop, which for the first time contains corn produced from genetically-altered seed.
Drazek was careful not to criticize the panel for the length of time it has taken to reach a final decision on the corn, but said, "I think they've been extremely methodical."

He would not speculate on what action the United States would take if EU does not approve the corn, and said that if the decision is based on scientific principles, "I have no reason to think it won't be (approved)."
